24 people on our team posted on LinkedIn using @PierreReddot's playbook. In 85 days, that helped us sign 27 new clients & $151K in new MRR.

We were clients of his agency at one point. It worked so well we took it in-house, and got him to teach the team too.

I had him on my YouTube a few months ago to go through how he makes his posts. What I took from it:

- A lot of his infographics are comparisons. B2B vs B2C, marketing vs sales lead systems, that kind of thing. He says "people love comparing stuff" and it helps them pick what's right for them

- On the episode we started an outbound one live in Canva. We kept the wrong side super basic on purpose (send a lot of emails, ask for a demo in email 1, big list) because he wanted it really obvious that's the wrong way, and the right side was supposed to be the long technical stuff. We didn't finish it but you get the idea

- Title as big as possible. People usually read the title, go top to bottom, and only read the caption if the graphic got them interested

- He adds a small note on the graphic for context. On his 4 levels of B2B marketing one, it just says "most businesses start here". Most people skip strategy and go straight to tactics, that's the point of it

- He guessed 60-70% of his posts start with a problem, agitate it, then give the fix. When he starts positive, he uses what he calls an "authority mark", like "I've been doing marketing for 10 years"

- No "comment to get the guide" posts. He wants his profile to feel like a safe place to learn. I still run plenty of those haha so not following this one

- Last one, probably the most true. He told us "you can have the best frameworks, best systems, but if people don't do it... the posts don't go live." For us the thing that made the team actually post was a quarterly competition with cash prizes (plus $500 for anyone who posted 20+ times in a quarter)

He's back on X now and says he'll teach this stuff here. Go give him a follow 👇

text:
I've sent 10M+ cold messages last year via my $7M ARR GTM agency. Now I spend more time cleaning my inbox than launching campaigns.

200+ pitches hit my inbox this month. I reply to almost none of them. But for a change, I went through this month's pile and pulled out the few I would actually engaged with. Four clear patterns showed up:

WHAT EARNS A REPLY

1. Real work, already done.
Some people offered to rewrite our landing pages. Others offered to draft sample scripts for our YouTube. We used to run this play in ColdIQ's early days, giving away custom lead lists for free, and got back more replies than we knew what to do with. Pro tip: imagine the prospect already signed. What's the first thing you'd ship for them? Do it already.

2. A specific internal referral ask.
If you've actually researched what we're working on at ColdIQ and figured out who owns it, I'll happily route you to the right person. You can scale this play by stacking buying signals in @clay with their "find person" feature to surface a colleague in a specific department.

3. A free insight, not a "free consultation."
The sharpest take on this came from Jihad Iqbal: the best "free work" isn't work, it's insights. A 5-minute technical audit. 3 specific optimization opportunities. No strings attached. Something like: "Your checkout flow has a 23% drop-off at payment verification. Here's why + 2 quick fixes." Takes 10 minutes. Shows instant value. Demonstrates expertise without asking for anything.

4. A notorious sender.
A bit unfair, but who sends the message matters as much as the message itself. If a public figure in your space (e.g. Alex Hormozi) sent you the worst LinkedIn DM ever, you'd still want to reply. I watched my own reply rates greatly increase as I built up my personal brand. Pro tip: if you're in B2B, build up your LinkedIn profile.

WHAT KILLS THE PITCH

1. "Can I pick your brain?"
I'd love to, but time is tight and there's little to no upside for me.

2. Copy-pasted templates.
Plenty of teams still run pure-volume plays, blasting the same template to everyone. Appealing to everyone = appealing to no one. You're wasting your DMs.

3. "Got 30 min for a quick sync?"
If the first thing you do is ask me for 30 min of my time, I'll find a way out.

text:
The exact 8-step system that helps us generate 20M+ impressions on LinkedIn (while also adding ~ $5M in ARR along the way):

1. Pick your ideal buyer.
> A lot of "viral" content doesn't convert because it's written for the creator's competitors, not their buyers. Understand your ICP and write content that serves them.

2. Map who actually surfaces it.
> Your buyer might not scroll. Their team does. Make something the team forwards up to them.

3. Audit before you write.
> Your own posts: which ones outperformed? Make more of those + variations.
> Competitor posts: how do you make them sharper, simpler, or better looking?
> Thought leaders in your niche: what's the quality gap, and how fast can you close it?

4. Build a swipe file.
> Pull outlier posts in your niche by author, keyword, or adjacent vertical. Taplio and Scripe do this in seconds.
> Adapt the format to your subject.

5. Lock 2-3 topics + a few recurring formats.
> Topics: AI agents, GTM tech.
> Formats: tools carousel, schema infographic.
> Run them weekly. Same topics, same formats, every week.
> Content doesn't need to be new. It needs to be shown to people who haven't seen it.

6. Rotate TOF / MOF / BOF.
> TOF: brings new people in
> MOF: piques interest in your offer
> BOF: drives action
> A single post rarely does all 3. Pick the goal before you publish.

7. Strong visuals = more reach.
> An image is worth 1,000 words. A video is thousands of images. Attention-grabbing designs always improve reach.

8. Hand the playbook to your team.
> You can't post 2+ times a day from one account without losing reach. But more posts = more total impressions.
> The fix: get your team posting too.

text:
Most people see one part of ColdIQ, usually the LinkedIn content, and assume that's the engine. It's not. The thing that pulls 55,000+ visits a month and supports $7M ARR has four layers:

marketing brings traffic in > lead capture turns it into pipeline > sales closes > and delivery scales the work without breaking.

1. Marketing (55,000+ visits/mo)

This is where the traffic enters. Five channels carry the load.

> LinkedIn (~15,000 visits/mo). The heaviest lifter. We have 20+ teammates publishing 150+ posts a month across outbound, AI, and GTM, with a combined audience of about 300K, designed in-house. Stack: Taplio, Scripe.

> SEO (~10,000 visits/mo). Yevhen runs programmatic SEO. Long-form blogs, programmatic landing pages on AirOps, and free micro-tools that Sacha builds in Claude Code. Stack: AirOps, Ahrefs, Claude Code, Webflow.

> Paid (~6,000 visits/mo). Ivan runs roughly $10K/mo across LinkedIn, Meta, and Google, mostly to test new channels rather than scale a winner. Stack: Claude Code, Fibbler, Usermaven.

> Cold outreach (~4,000 visits/mo). Kenny runs internal campaigns off tight lists of fewer than 5,000 deeply enriched contacts at a time, rotating between value-driven lead magnets, lookalike account targeting, social engagement plays, and inbound-led outbound. Stack: Clay, Claude Code, Apollo, Instantly, lemlist, Prospeo, FullEnrich, CompanyEnrich, PredictLeads.

> Newsletter, webinars, and emerging channels (~11,000 visits/mo). Monika ships the beehiiv newsletter. Harry runs the webinars. TikTok, Instagram, and X are newer experiments growing share fast.

2. Lead capture

Traffic alone doesn't convert, so lead capture is its own layer sitting on top of marketing.

> Midbound and Vector surface anonymous visitors.
> Customer .io handles lifecycle emails.
> Micro-tools and pop-up lead magnets quietly collect emails.
> Everything routes through n8n and gets scored in real time by Clay, OpenAI, and PredictLeads before a salesperson ever sees it.
